triage.summary: Your database's bounds are order sqrt(KT log(K/delta)) above and sqrt(KT log(1/delta)) below (Gerchinovitz & Lattimore 2016), a sqrt(log K) gap at fixed delta. A 2026 arXiv preprint (Bacchiocchi, Cesari, Colomboni, 2608.12231, v2 25 Aug 2026) proves the matching lower bound in its Theorem 2. For any algorithm, a deterministic adaptive adversary with losses in [0,1] forces P(R_T >= c*sqrt(dT(log C(d,m) + log(1/delta)))) >= delta. This holds for delta <= delta_0 (a universal constant whose value the paper does not give) and T above a threshold polynomial in d, m and log(1/delta). With m=1 this is Omega(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))). The authors say this closes the remaining log K gap left by Gerchinovitz & Lattimore. Their algorithm's upper bound, O(sqrt(KT log(K/delta))), matches EXP3-KW, so the bound is tight up to constants. Caveats: (1) the lower bound needs an adaptive (non-anticipating) adversary, and the paper does not settle the oblivious case, where the only known lower bound remains sqrt(KT log(1/delta)); (2) the result is for confidence-tuned algorithms (delta fixed in advance); (3) it is a single, very recent preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I can tell. Gerchinovitz & Lattimore themselves (full text read) do not mention the log K gap or call it open. I tried to check Audibert & Bubeck's JMLR 2010 and COLT 2009 PDFs for a high-probability bound without log K under oblivious adversaries, but neither PDF rendered, so that question is unchecked.

triage.summary:
The gap is closed up to iterated-log factors, and the paper that closes it is the one the database already takes its lower bound from: Li, Wang & Zhou (COLT 2019, arXiv:1904.00242).

**Setting.** Linear contextual bandits with adversarial, time-varying finite action sets of size n.

**Lower bound.** The paper proves Ω(√(dT log T log n)) for n ≤ 2^{d/2}, valid when T ≥ d(log₂ n)^{1+ε}. Taking n = 2^{d/2} recovers the database's Ω(d√(T log T)); that substitution is my own inference, the paper does not state it.

**Upper bound.** The same paper's Variable-Confidence-Level (VCL) SupLinUCB algorithm "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors". That gives O(√(dT log T log n)·poly(log log T)), which saves two √log T factors over earlier SupLinUCB analyses. The database instead lists LinTS (Agrawal & Goyal 2013), which is much looser.

**What remains open.** Only a poly(log log T) gap. If the database insists on exact log tightness, "open_known (log log gap)" would be the stricter label.

**Caveats.**
- I read only the abstract and search summaries, not the paper's theorem statements. The explicit form √(dT log T log n)·poly(log log T) is inferred from the abstract's "matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithmic factors" and a talk abstract by Yuan Zhou.
- I didn't check whether the upper bound's analysis needs any extra assumption beyond this setting, e.g. knowing σ.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00242 ; https://proceedings.mlr.press/v99/li19b.html ; https://itcs.sufe.edu.cn/41/5b/c10453a213339/page.htm

triage.summary:
I found no source that closes this gap or calls it a known open problem for this exact setting. The setting is a fixed finite action set of K points, oblivious adversary, losses in the polar of the action set, and expected regret.

The setting's upper bound is O(√(dT log K)) (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi and Kakade, 2012, Theorem 4). Its abstract presents this only as an upper bound. It calls the d√(T log T) bound for compact action sets "minimax optimal up to a logarithmic factor", but makes no such claim for the √(dT log K) bound.

The only K-dependent lower bound I confirmed for a fixed action set is for K = 2^d. Shamir (2015), in the dual normalization, proves an Ω((d−1)√T) lower bound for the hypercube [−1,1]^d (Theorem 6, which needs T ≥ d⁴/4). Because the losses are linear, this also applies to the corner set {−1,1}^d, where d√T is the same order as √(dT log K). It also cites a prior Ω(d√T) lower bound for the Boolean hypercube. Two caveats: Shamir allows sub-Gaussian loss noise rather than strictly bounded losses, and says this relaxation costs only a √log T factor in lower bounds. At K = d (the simplex), Shamir's Ω(√(dT)) lower bound matches EXP3, and no log K term appears.

So √log K is needed at the extreme K = 2^d (up to the noise-model caveat), but I found no lower bound for general K.

The most relevant candidate is Ito (NeurIPS 2024), "On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice". Its abstract states an upper bound of O(√(dT log(K·min{1, S/d}))) with a matching lower bound, where S is the number of contexts. With S = 1 this would give Θ(√(dT log(K/d))) and close the gap. However, I could not read the full text: the PDF did not extract and OpenReview was blocked by a browser check. I therefore could not confirm that the lower bound covers S = 1, nor its loss normalization or adversary model. It may need S ≥ d.

Bacchiocchi, Cesari and Colomboni (arXiv 2608.12231) prove a matching lower bound of order √(dT log(K/δ)). But it is a high-probability bound against adaptive adversaries for m-set bandits, so it does not settle the expected-regret question. Li et al. (2019), Ω(√(dT log K log T)), is for stochastic contextual bandits whose action sets change over time; I saw it only cited secondhand and did not fetch it.

The verdict is "blank" because Ito (2024) could not be checked. If its lower bound covers S = 1 under bounded polar losses, the verdict should be "closed".

The Dani-Hayes-Kakade abstract claims the price of bandit information is at least sqrt(n), which against sqrt(nT) full-information regret means Omega(n sqrt T) bandit regret. I could not read their PDF, so their exact theorem, decision set and constant are unverified; that the construction is the bounded-loss cube comes from the 2012 paper's citation. Shamir (2015), Theorem 6, gives c(d-1)sqrt(T) on [-1,1]^d for T >= d^4/4 with stochastic losses whose mean lies in the l1 ball and whose tails are sub-Gaussian, not bounded by 1. So the d-exponent gap (1 vs 0.5) closes at Theta(d sqrt T); the database is missing the Omega(d sqrt T) lower bound.

triage.summary: I count the √(log K) gap as closed, by a direct consequence of a published result rather than a theorem stated for this setting. The database's upper bound √(2 K M T log K) comes from running EXP3 separately in each context. Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009 / JMLR 2010) give INF, which removes the log K factor and gets O(√(nK)) minimax regret in the adversarial K-armed bandit. Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) also matches the minimax bound within constants. Running INF or Tsallis-INF per context and applying Cauchy–Schwarz (∑_c √T_c ≤ √(M T)) gives O(√(K M T)), which matches the Ω(√(KT)) lower bound in K and T. A standard block construction would also give Ω(√(K M T)) in M, but that is my own derivation: I didn't find it stated in a paper or in the sources I read. Caveats: INF's guarantee is for pseudo-regret / expected regret against an oblivious adversary, so check that this matches the database's regret notion. I took the Audibert–Bubeck claim from search-result summaries and did not fetch the full text, so the theorem number and constant are unchecked. triage.summary: Closed in the worst-case-over-instances sense. Theorem 8 of Bubeck, Perchet and Rigollet (COLT 2013, arXiv:1302.1611), read from a text version of the arXiv PDF fetched through the r.jina.ai proxy, covers two arms, unit-variance Gaussians and a learner that knows only mu*. Instances: nu0 = N(0,1) x N(-1,1) and nu_Delta = N(-Delta,1) x N(0,1) for Delta in (0,1], so mu* = 0 throughout. Statement: for any policy and any n, max(R_n(nu0), sup_Delta Delta*R_n(nu_Delta)) >= (1/2) log(n/139). The paper reads this as 'regret of order log(n)/Delta is unavoidable for some Delta when only mu* is known'. My own step, not stated in the paper: since R_n(nu_Delta) <= n*Delta, the Delta attaining the sup has n*Delta^2 >~ log n, so log n ~ log(1/Delta). Hence no uniform guarantee of order C/Delta, or o(log(1/Delta))/Delta, is possible, and the log(1/Delta)/Delta upper bound (Garivier, Menard and Stoltz 2019, Theorem C.1, taken from the database; I could not read that PDF) is order-optimal in Delta. A per-instance log(1/Delta)/Delta lower bound cannot hold, because an algorithm tuned to one Delta gets order 1/Delta there, so the per-instance 1/(4 Delta) from Theorem 5 (where Delta is also known) remains correct. The K 'poly_gap' is a bookkeeping artefact since K = 2 is fixed. Several fetches failed: the raw arXiv PDFs of 1302.1611 (v1, v2) and 1602.07182 and the PMLR PDF would not extract, and sbubeck.com refused the connection. The r.jina.ai text version of 1302.1611 worked.

Theorem 5, where both mu* and Delta are known, gives the 1/Delta-order lower bound.

triage.summary: Li, Wang and Zhou (COLT 2019) close this gap up to iterated-logarithm factors. The setting is finite-armed linear contextual bandits with K arms per round and adversarially chosen (oblivious) action sets. Their lower bound is Ω(√(dT log T log K)), proved for K ≤ 2^{d/2} under a horizon condition. Their VCL-SupLinUCB algorithm has an upper bound of O(√(dT log T log K))·poly(log log(KT)). This is two √log T factors better than SupLinUCB's bound of √(dT log^3(KT)), the upper bound in our database. The lower bound is also stronger than the database's √(dT) lower bound. The only remaining gap is a poly(log log) factor. The database's per-variable T-exponent gap (log^1.5 against 0.5) should be updated to: upper √(T log T)·polyloglog, lower √(T log T). One caveat: the lower bound needs K ≤ 2^{d/2}. A related recent paper, Jin (arXiv 2609.15170), studies action sets chosen adaptively, which is a different setting from the oblivious sequence here. Its bounds include a K^{1/4} factor, so it does not apply.

However, they need a 'smooth rewards' condition: R_a − R_b must be ρ(a,b)-sub-Gaussian, plus separability. Generic bounded ±1 noise that is independent across actions does not satisfy this, so the result does not cover this setting as stated. The follow-up arXiv:2502.02140 still has d√(T log T). On the lower-bound side, Li-Wang-Zhou (COLT 2019) prove Ω(√(dT log T log n)) only for action sets that change every round (contextual), which does not transfer to a fixed action set. No source I saw states the fixed-action-set, bounded-noise case as an explicit open problem, hence 'blank'. The gap looks closed in spirit, but only under an extra assumption.

(1) Zimmert & Lattimore (COLT 2022), "Return of the Bias", prove a high-probability regret bound of O(d sqrt(T log(T/δ))) for adversarial linear bandits on general action sets. The algorithm is FTRL with a log-determinant potential. The bound holds against adaptive adversaries, so it covers the oblivious case. This lowers the d exponent of the upper bound from 2.5 to 1. Their lower bound may need a specific convex body (e.g. a hypercube with losses bounded by |<a,y>|<=1), in which case the match holds for some convex bodies rather than every one. (b) I did not see a lower bound combining the d sqrt(T) order with a log(1/δ) term, so the δ-dependence is only matched up to log factors. papers.claim: Against an adaptive adversary, regret O(d√(T log(T/δ))) holds with probability ≥1−δ for general action sets. The efficient entropic-barrier FTRL version gets d²√T log T, improving on Lee et al. 2020's d^{7/2}√T polylog(T).

papers.claim: Theorem 6: on the hypercube W=[-1,1]^d with sub-Gaussian valid losses, regret ≥ c(d−1)√T for T ≥ d⁴/4. The bound transfers to strictly bounded losses at a √log T cost.

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: Per the abstract: lower bounds showing the bandit vs full-information regret gap is at least √n, where n is the dimension (classic linear-bandit lower bound). Only the abstract was read; the exact theorem was not checked.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to a sqrt(log T) factor. Zimmert & Lattimore (COLT 2022) show minimax regret O(d sqrt(T log T)) against adaptive adversaries, which also holds with high probability, for general (convex) action sets. That improves the database's d^2.5 upper bound to d^1. The matching Omega(d sqrt T) lower bound comes from Dani, Hayes & Kakade (2008). It holds even for oblivious adversaries, so it applies here. I saw this lower bound only as cited by Bubeck's blog and by Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade (arXiv 1110.4322); I did not fetch the 2008 paper itself. Its exact convex body and loss set were not checked against the polar-loss-set convention. In d the bounds now match (exponent 1); in T only a sqrt(log T) factor remains.

papers.title: Return of the Bias: Almost Minimax Optimal High Probability Bounds for Adversarial Linear Bandits
papers.claim: Minimax regret for adaptive adversarial linear bandits is at most O(d sqrt(T log T)); high-probability O(d sqrt(T log(T/delta))); efficient entropic-barrier FTRL gets O(d^2 sqrt(T) log T) against adaptive adversaries.

papers.title: The Price of Bandit Information for Online Optimization (Dani, Hayes, Kakade)
papers.claim: Seen only as cited in secondary sources (Bubeck blog; Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Kakade): there is an action set (and prior) with regret Omega(d sqrt T) for any strategy. This is a lower bound for linear bandits.

papers.title: Towards Minimax Policies for Online Linear Optimization with Bandit Feedback / An Optimal Algorithm for Linear Bandits (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi, Kakade)
papers.claim: Regret of order d sqrt(T) (up to logs) for infinite action sets against oblivious adversaries; states such bounds cannot be improved in general.

triage.summary:
The √log T gap is closed, apart from iterated-logarithm (log log) factors, by the same paper the database already cites for its lower bound. That paper is Li, Wang & Zhou, "Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits" (COLT 2019, arXiv:1904.00242).

**Setting:** linear contextual bandits with finite action sets of n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per round, chosen adversarially and changing each round.

**What the paper shows:**
- **Lower bound:** minimax regret is Ω(√(dT log T log n)).
- **Upper bound:** their Variable-Confidence-Level SupLinUCB algorithm matches this lower bound up to iterated-logarithm factors, removing two √log T factors from earlier SupLinUCB analyses.
- **Infinite or very large action sets:** a talk abstract by co-author Yuan Zhou says the paper also gives O(d√(T log T))·poly(log log T), matching Ω(d√(T log T)) up to log log factors.

**Why the database shows a gap:** the stored upper bound is the weaker Thompson-sampling bound (Agrawal & Goyal 2013). The tight upper bound from Theorem-level results in Li–Wang–Zhou is missing from the database.

**Caveats:**
- The rates hold only up to poly(log log T) factors, so the gap is closed in T and d except for log log terms.
- I only read the arXiv abstract and search summaries, not the theorem statements. In particular, the abstract does not state the upper bound explicitly; it only says the algorithm matches the lower bound up to iterated logarithms.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Yingkai Li, Yining Wang, Yuan Zhou)
papers.claim: For linear contextual bandits with n ≤ 2^{d/2} actions per period, minimax regret is Ω(√(dT log T log n)); the VCL SupLinUCB algorithm matches this up to iterated-log factors. Per a co-author's talk abstract, for infinite action sets the upper bound is O(d√(T log T))·poly(log log T), matching the Ω(d√(T log T)) lower bound.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to constants by results missing from the database. Only abstracts and search snippets were checked, not full PDFs. Upper bound: Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, JMLR 2021) gets regret O(sum_i log T/Delta_i + sqrt(C sum_i log T/Delta_i)) in a setting that includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruption. This is linear in K, has a single log T, matches the Lai-Robbins log T/Delta rate at C=0, and is at most O(sum log T/Delta_i + C) by AM-GM. That removes the extra K and log T factors in the Lykouris et al. 2018 bound. Masoudian & Seldin (COLT 2021) refine the log factor and the C dependence. Lower bound: Ito (NeurIPS 2021) proves a bandit lower bound tight up to a log factor; a search summary gives it as Omega(N/Delta + sqrt(CN/Delta)), N = number of arms, but the exact expression was not seen. With Lai-Robbins this shows the sqrt(C...) shape is near-optimal. Caveats: (1) the KL-based Lai-Robbins bound matches log T/Delta only up to constants when arm means are bounded away from 0 and 1; (2) I believe, but did not confirm in the papers, that Zimmert-Seldin's setting allows adaptive adversaries and bounds regret against corrupted losses; (3) Ito's bandit lower bound leaves a log-factor gap in the C-dependent term only, not in the K, log T or Delta gaps listed for this setting.

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits (Zimmert, Seldin)
papers.claim: Regret O(sum_i log T/Delta_i + sqrt(C sum_i log T/Delta_i)) in a setting that includes stochastic bandits with adversarial corruptions.

papers.title: Improved Analysis of the Tsallis-INF Algorithm in Stochastically Constrained Adversarial Bandits and Stochastic Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions (Masoudian, Seldin)
papers.claim: Replaces log T with log((K-1)T/(sum 1/Delta_i)^2) and improves the dependence on corruption C.

papers.title: On Optimal Robustness to Adversarial Corruption in Online Decision Problems (Ito)
papers.claim: Tight bound (log N)/Delta + sqrt(C log N/Delta) for experts; for bandits, a lower bound tight up to a log factor, reported in a search summary as Omega(N/Delta + sqrt(CN/Delta)) (exact form not seen), showing Tsallis-INF is nearly optimal.

triage.summary: I found no published result that closes the gap for Bayesian regret (worst case over priors) in stochastic linear bandits with a fixed, arbitrary compact action set. I also found no paper that explicitly calls this Bayesian version open. The upper bound can be tightened from the database's d√T·log T (Russo & Van Roy) to d√(T log T). This rate comes from Dong & Van Roy 2018 (rate-distortion analysis of Thompson sampling); I saw the explicit form quoted by Gouverneur et al. 2025, who recover the same rate with better constants inside the log. That leaves a √(log T) gap against the d√T lower bound (Dani et al.; Lattimore–Szepesvári Theorem 24.2). Li, Wang & Zhou 2019 prove Ω(d√(T log T)), but only for action sets that change over time, so it does not apply to a fixed set. Fixed sets are settled only for special shapes: Zhang, Hadiji & Combes 2025 get minimax-optimal Θ(d√T) with no log factor for ellipsoids. Banerjee & Gopalan 2023 say earlier work called characterizing minimax regret across action spaces open, but that is the frequentist question. I could not get the text of the Lattimore–Szepesvári chapter notes to check for an explicit open-problem statement.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis for Thompson Sampling with Many Actions (Dong, Van Roy)
papers.claim: Rate-distortion analysis of Thompson sampling giving near-optimal Bayesian regret for linear bandits. Gouverneur et al. quote the rate as O(d√(T log T)), which beats the database's d√T log T upper bound.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Thompson Sampling with Infinite Action Spaces (Gouverneur, Rodriguez Gálvez, Oechtering, Skoglund)
papers.claim: Recovers the O(d√(T log T)) Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling for linear bandits with infinite action spaces and improves the constants inside the log. No log-free bound.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits (Li, Wang, Zhou)
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(d√(T log T)) for infinite action sets, but the sets change over time. Does not apply to a fixed compact action set.

papers.title: Linear Bandits on Ellipsoids: Minimax Optimal Algorithms (Zhang, Hadiji, Combes)
papers.claim: Matching upper and lower bounds of order dσ√T (up to universal constants) for ellipsoidal action sets, with no log T. Covers only one special shape, not arbitrary compact sets.

papers.title: On the Minimax Regret for Linear Bandits in a wide variety of Action Spaces (Banerjee, Gopalan)
papers.claim: Optimal regret lower bound for a broad class of convex action spaces. Says earlier work noted that characterizing minimax regret across action spaces was an open problem (frequentist setting).

triage.summary:
The √log K gap is closed, but only by combining two published results. I did not find a paper that states the contextual bound itself.

Setting: M_ctx finite contexts chosen by an oblivious adversary, K arms, rewards in [0,1]. The database upper bound, √(2·K·M·T·log K), comes from running a separate Exp3 for each context.

**Upper bound without the log factor.** Replace Exp3 with Tsallis-INF (Zimmert & Seldin, arXiv 1807.07623). Its Theorem 1 bounds adversarial pseudo-regret by 4√(KT)+1 with importance-weighted estimators. The bound is anytime: the learning rate is η_t = 2/√t, so it needs neither T nor a doubling scheme. That matters here because each context's round count T_c is unknown in advance. Running one copy per context gives regret at most Σ_c(4√(K·T_c)+1). By Cauchy–Schwarz this is at most 4√(K·M·T)+M, which is O(√(KMT)) when T ≥ M. Against an oblivious adversary, pseudo-regret and expected regret coincide. Audibert & Bubeck's INF (COLT 2009 / JMLR 2010) already removed the √log K factor for the non-contextual problem.

**Matching lower bound.** Split the rounds into M blocks of T/M, one block per context, and apply the existing √((K−1)T)/504 bound to each block. This gives Ω(√(MKT)). Note that the lower bounds in the database omit the M factor.

So the minimax rate is Θ(√(KMT)): it is tight in K, M and T up to constants.

**Caveats.**
- I found no paper that explicitly states the composed O(√(KMT)) bound for this setting.
- I could not read the text of Lattimore & Szepesvári Chapter 18 ("One bandit per context"). The fetched PDF came back as unreadable binary, so I could not check whether the book makes this remark or poses it as an exercise.
- Neither of the two composition steps is spelled out in a paper I found. The anytime per-context argument and the block-splitting lower bound are my own reasoning. They are standard arguments, but I have not seen them written down this session.

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits (Zimmert, Seldin; JMLR 2021)
papers.claim: Theorem 1: anytime adversarial pseudo-regret ≤ 4√(KT)+1 (IW estimators), learning rate η_t=2/√t, no horizon knowledge needed. Running one copy per context gives O(√(KMT)), removing the √log K factor.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits (Audibert, Bubeck; COLT 2009) / Regret Bounds and Minimax Policies under Partial Monitoring (JMLR 2010)
papers.claim: INF with a polynomial ψ removes the extraneous log factor in the adversarial bandit pseudo-regret, giving the minimax rate Θ(√(KT)) for non-contextual bandits.

triage.summary: The log K gap is closed: minimax regret for oblivious adversarial K-armed bandits is Θ(√(KT)). Audibert & Bubeck (COLT 2009; JMLR 2010) introduced the INF forecaster and, per the search results, removed the extra log factor from Exp3's √(KT log K) bound. Zimmert & Seldin's Tsallis-INF (Tsallis entropy, α=1/2) also reaches O(√(KT)) adversarial regret, within a factor <15 of the minimax lower bound. The search snippets did not show the explicit √(nK) statement or exact constants for either paper. Losses in [-1,1] instead of [0,1] change only constants, so the K-exponent is tight at 0.5 against the Ω(√(T(K−1))) lower bounds.

papers.title: Minimax Policies for Adversarial and Stochastic Bandits (Audibert, Bubeck)
papers.claim: Per the search results, removes the extraneous log factor from the √(nK log K) Exp3 upper bound via the INF (implicitly normalized forecaster) family; the explicit √(nK) statement and constant were not seen in the snippets.

papers.title: Regret Bounds and Minimax Policies under Partial Monitoring (Audibert, Bubeck), JMLR 11
papers.claim: Journal version: the INF forecaster with ψ(x)=(η/−x)^q+γ/K removes the extraneous logarithmic factor in pseudo-regret bounds for adversarial bandits.

papers.title: Tsallis-INF: An Optimal Algorithm for Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits (Zimmert, Seldin)
papers.claim: Tsallis entropy with α=1/2 gives minimax-optimal O(√(KT)) adversarial regret; with a reduced-variance estimator it is within a factor <15 of the minimax lower bound.

triage.summary: The gap is closed up to logarithmic factors. The database's best upper bound (Lee et al. 2020, scaling as K^2) is far from the best known. The classic Exp3.P (Auer et al. 2002), written up in Bubeck & Cesa-Bianchi's survey (arXiv:1204.5721, §3.2), gives regret ≤ 5.15·sqrt(KT·log(K/δ)) with probability ≥ 1−δ. The survey's theorem statement was not read directly: the 5.15 constant and its attribution come from citing papers (arXiv:1812.04152, and Neu 2015, which says it improves on that constant). Neu's Exp3-IX (arXiv:1506.03271) also gets high-probability regret of order sqrt(KT) without forced exploration; its exact δ-dependence was not checked. Against the Gerchinovitz–Lattimore lower bound sqrt(T(K−1)log(1/(4δ)))/27, the K exponent is 1/2 on both sides, so the bounds match up to sqrt(log K) and constants. The apparent poly gap comes from the database missing Exp3.P and Exp3-IX.

papers.title: Regret Analysis of Stochastic and Nonstochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problems (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi)
papers.claim: Exp3.P: with probability ≥ 1−δ, regret ≤ 5.15·sqrt(nK·log(K/δ)) (Theorem 3.2, Sec. 3.2). The constant comes from citing papers; the theorem itself was not read.

papers.title: Explore no more: Improved high-probability regret bounds for non-stochastic bandits (Neu)
papers.claim: Exp3-IX gets high-probability regret of order sqrt(KT) (up to logs) without explicit exploration, improving on Exp3.P's constants. Seen only via abstract and summaries.

triage.summary: No source found closes the √log K gap, and none explicitly calls it open. The setting is fixed finite-action (K actions, d dims) adversarial oblivious linear bandits, expected regret. Upper bound O(√(dT log K)) (Bubeck et al. 2012; Dann et al. 2023); lower bound Ω(√(dT)). Closest results: (1) Bacchiocchi, Cesari & Colomboni (arXiv 2608.12231) prove a matching Ω(√(dT log(K/δ))) lower bound, but it is high-probability and against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries, so not this setting. Their related work gives the best expected-regret m-set lower bound as Ω(√(dmT)) under action-level normalization (attributed to Ito et al., not seen directly). This matches √(dT log K) only up to a log(d/m) factor and uses a coordinate-wise loss normalization that does not map directly to unit-ℓ2 actions with an ℓ2-ball parameter. The paper does not discuss whether the expected-regret gap is open. (2) Liu, Li & Lui (arXiv 2608.14319) list the classical finite-action linear bandit bounds as O(√(dT log K)) vs Ω(√(dT)), the latter via the d-armed embedding. This is a stochastic-case summary but suggests no sharper K-dependent lower bound is standard. (3) Li, Wang & Zhou (arXiv 1904.00242) prove Ω(√(dT log T log K)) only for stochastic contextual bandits with time-varying action sets; it cannot transfer to fixed action sets. I could not access the Lattimore–Szepesvári book notes on finite action sets. The Dani–Hayes–Kakade 2007 search results show no K-dependent lower bound.

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial m-Set Bandits
papers.claim: High-probability regret O(√(dT log(K/δ))) with a matching Ω(√(dT log(K/δ))) high-probability lower bound against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries. Related work cites an expected-regret m-set lower bound of Ω(√(dmT)) after rescaling (Ito et al.), which is weaker than √(dT log K) by a √log(d/m) factor. Not the oblivious expected-regret setting.

papers.title: Quantum Multi-Armed Bandits and Linear Bandits: Lower Bounds and Algorithms
papers.claim: Table 1 lists classical finite-action linear bandits as UB O(√(dT log K)) (Lattimore–Szepesvári Ch. 22) vs LB Ω(√(dT)) via the standard d-armed embedding. Stochastic setting; the gap is not called open.

papers.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Regret for Linearly Parameterized Bandits
papers.claim: Lower bound Ω(√(dT log T log K)) for stochastic linear contextual bandits with time-varying action sets (K ≤ 2^{d/2}). Does not apply to fixed action sets.
